nutshell: Event cameras were assumed privacy-preserving because their sparse output is hard for humans to interpret, but neural networks can still reconstruct images and re-identify people from event streams. AnonyNoise trains a lightweight noise-prediction network to anonymize raw event data against neural-network re-identification specifically (not just human viewing), using adversarial min-max training against a continuously-updated re-ID attacker network while a separate target network keeps the data usable for gesture/emotion recognition.
contributions: The first anonymization pipeline for event data explicitly targeting re-identification by neural networks (rather than only preventing human-interpretable image reconstruction, which is what the prior closest work, Ahmad et al. ICCV'23, addressed).

A learnable, data-dependent Gaussian noise mechanism: the anonymization network predicts a per-pixel mean and standard deviation from the raw event histogram plus an injected noise input, combined via the reparameterization trick - shown to anonymize more effectively than fixed-variance Gaussian noise at matched target-task accuracy.

A min-max adversarial training pipeline where the re-identification attacker network is continuously updated (not frozen) during anonymization training, explicitly to guard against an attacker that retrains after anonymization is deployed - plus a separate post-training stage that simulates exactly that retraining attack for evaluation.

Empirical robustness checks beyond the primary re-ID metric: generalization to an unseen dataset (Event-ReId, different camera setup, no fine-tuning) and resistance to an inversion attack (a trained denoising network) and to image reconstruction via a pretrained E2VID model.
deficiencies: The headline privacy-reduction numbers are computed inconsistently across the two main datasets: for DVS-Gesture the '~60%' figure is a relative reduction in re-ID accuracy (98.33%→40.00%, actually a 59.3% relative drop), but for SEE the '~50%' figure reads as the raw percentage-point drop (72.5%→25.0%, which is actually a 65.5% relative reduction) - the two headline numbers aren't computed the same way, which risks misleading a reader comparing them directly.

On SEE, the target-task accuracy cost is understated by the framing: it drops from 77.14% to 55.71% (a 21-point absolute drop on a 7-class task), described merely as 'reducing it by 22%' in the same sentence as DVS-Gesture's much smaller accuracy cost (92.42%→80.68%) - these are not comparably minor utility losses, and 55.71% on 7-way emotion classification leaves much less headroom above chance than the framing suggests.

The cross-dataset generalization result (Table 2, Event-ReId) still leaves substantial re-identification risk in absolute terms: top-1 accuracy only falls from 59.09% to 38.64% (an attacker still correctly identifies more than a third of queries) and top-10 accuracy remains 68.18% - a meaningful relative improvement over no protection, but not a strong absolute privacy guarantee for a real deployment.

The image-reconstruction-attack claim ('robust against grayscale reconstruction') rests on a single qualitative example (Fig. 3c, one DVS-Gesture sample) with no quantitative reconstruction-quality metric (e.g. SSIM/PSNR/LPIPS against ground truth) reported in the main paper, which is thin evidence for a claim listed among the paper's core robustness results.

All datasets are small (DVS-Gesture: 6 test subjects; SEE: 20 validation subjects with exactly one sample per emotion each; Event-ReId: 11 test subjects) with no repeated-run variance reporting anywhere, so the reported percentage changes rest on very few identities per split.
notable: The ablation in Table 3 has a genuinely counterintuitive result worth flagging: adding a learned mean offset to the output without the stochastic noise term (input Xe, output Xe+Xμ) barely anonymizes at all - re-ID accuracy actually rises to 83.33% (worse than several fixed-noise baselines) even though target accuracy stays reasonably high (81.82%). This suggests the stochastic noise component, not the learned deterministic shift, is doing essentially all of the actual privacy-preserving work in this architecture - a useful negative result for anyone designing a similar noise-prediction anonymizer.
